# Retrofitted Recurrence: Teaching Pretrained Language Models to Think Deeper with Retrofitted Recurrence

English · [简体中文](../zh/2511.07384.md) · [Back to the list](../../README.md)

<sub>arXiv 2511.07384 · 2025-11-10 · University of Maryland, New York University, Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, University of North Carolina, ELLIS Institute Tübingen, Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems, Tübingen AI Center, Columbia University</sub>

<img src="../../assets/glyphs/2511.07384.svg" alt="L0-3 (4 layers) -&gt; [L10-17 (8 layers)] x Poisson-Lognormal, mean ramped to 4, 8, 16 or 32 -&gt; L18-21 (4 layers); injection concat; KV n/a">

> Turn pretrained 1B models into prelude-core-coda recurrent models by dropping middle layers and looping a block, then keep training while a curriculum raises the mean recurrence.

**Category**: Training and retrofitting · **Status**: draft (numbers not yet re-checked) · **Impact**: cites 82 · stars 73 · HF upvotes 21

[paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.07384) · [code](https://github.com/mcleish7/retrofitting-recurrence) · [weights](https://huggingface.co/collections/tomg-group-umd/retrofitting-recurrence)

## Problem

Pretraining a depth-recurrent model from scratch is costly. Huginn-0125 used 800B tokens, and running many recurrences per step slows training compared with a fixed-depth model of the same parameter count. The paper studies how to convert existing pretrained non-recurrent models into recurrent ones efficiently.

## Method

- Take a pretrained model's early layers as the prelude and later layers as the recurrent core and coda, dropping the layers in between, e.g. (4,8,4) from TinyLlama-1.1B-3T and (4,6,4) from OLMo-2-0425-1B and Llama-3.2-1B.
- Keep Huginn-0125's recurrence, with a linear adapter on concat(prelude output, state), a random initial state, a Poisson-Lognormal recurrence count and gradients through at most the last 8 core passes.
- Raise the mean of the recurrence distribution with a curriculum (1-sqrt over the first 75% of training in the main runs) to 4, 8, 16 or 32, and optimize with Muon.
- Train on about 50B tokens of Nemotron-CC-Math-v1-4plus. To keep general ability, first heal on 26B tokens of FineWeb-Edu, then train on 26B tokens mixing FineWeb-Edu with Nemotron SFT data.

## Loop layout

| Facet | Value |
|---|---|
| Where the loop sits | middle core (prelude-core-coda) |
| Weight sharing | fully tied |
| Passes in training | scheduled curriculum |
| Passes at test time | can run more passes than trained |
| Input injection | concat + projection |
| KV cache | n/a |
| Gradient through passes | truncated (last k passes) |
| Origin | retrofitted from a pretrained model |
| FFN | dense FFN |
| Attention in the loop | full attention |
| Passes (L10-17) | train Poisson-Lognormal, mean ramped to 4, 8, 16 or 32; test 1-32 |
| Backprop (L10-17) | last 8 |

Shown is TinyLlama (4,8,4); labels are layer indices in the 22-layer TinyLlama-1.1B-3T parent, whose layers 4-9 are dropped. OLMo-2-0425-1B and Llama-3.2-1B use (4,6,4) with layers L0-3, L6-11 and L12-15, dropping L4-5. Sections 4.1-4.2 use a (2,4,2) model built from Llama-3.2-1B. The recurrence count is sampled from a Poisson-Lognormal distribution whose mean follows the curriculum, so depth is both sampled and scheduled.

## Other findings

- Linearly ramping the mean recurrence up to 32 slightly lowers validation loss per step and greatly lowers it per training FLOP ((2,4,2) from Llama, 48 hours on 4 MI300A GPUs, about 1e20 FLOPs). (Section 4.2; Figure 3)
- On GSM8K, larger training recurrences give a larger gain per training FLOP for OLMo and Llama, but not for TinyLlama. (Section 4.3.2; Figure 20)
- A 26B-token FineWeb-Edu healing phase before the mixed data raises the recurrent model's Arc-C by 5% over single-phase training, while the non-recurrent model changes little. (Section 4.4; Figure 8)
- Among the tested layer choices for a (2,4,2) model from Llama-1b, taking early layers for the prelude and later layers for the core and coda gave the lowest training loss; on TinyLlama (4,8,4) this choice also reached lower loss than layers picked with ShortGPT. (Appendix C.1.1; Figures 12 and 13)
- Muon trains the recurrent models more stably than AdamW, whose loss spiked to NaN at learning rate 5e-5; for the non-recurrent TinyLlama the gap is much smaller, with a small gain for Muon. (Section 4.3.1; Figure 4)

## Comparison

- **Baseline**: The parent model (TinyLlama, OLMo or Llama) post-trained without recurrence on the same data in the same order. Figures 5-7 compare accuracy against training FLOPs and at the final checkpoint.
- **Held fixed**: D (training tokens)
- **Differs**: N (unique parameters), F (training FLOPs), L (executed layers per token)
- **Baseline hyperparameters**: shared with the looped model
- **Headline claim**: Converting a pretrained model to a recurrent one gives better math accuracy at a given training compute budget than post-training the non-recurrent model. After the same ~50B math tokens, OLMo (4,6,4) at train and test recurrence 32 scores 51.6 on GSM8K and 29.3 on MATH, against 35.3 and 25.1 for the post-trained non-recurrent OLMo. (Abstract; Section 4.3; Table 4)

## Caveats

- Models have about 1B parameters and are post-trained on about 50B tokens (about 120B in the initialization study); the authors say larger model and data scales still need testing.
- All models are trained with a 1024-token context.
- Against the non-recurrent parent, data and tokens are matched but parameters and compute are not. The recurrent models keep 72.7% (TinyLlama) or 87.5% (OLMo, Llama) of the parent's parameters and use more FLOPs per training step.
- All models share one hyperparameter set (Muon with learning rate 0.001 and weight decay 1e-4, Appendix D); the baselines are not tuned separately.
- Training only on math slightly lowers HellaSwag, Arc and OpenBookQA (Section 4.4). GSM8K and MATH use one in-context example, flexible extract for GSM8K and Minerva criteria with Math-Verify for MATH.
